title: “Prowling” Media Goons
author: Peter Byrne
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-27-at-4.26.02-PM-680x459.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/28/prowling-
media-goons/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-27-at-4.26.02-PM-680x459.png)

Photo by [Matt
C](https://unsplash.com/@mchesin?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

Elaine Forbes, the former San Francisco Port Commission’s Executive Director
and (currently on-leave) Sausalito City Manager, was arraigned on Wednesday in
Marin County Superior Court on four misdemeanor counts. None of the
misdemeanors Forbes is charged with involved any violence or physical harm,
unless you count the self-inflicted damaged of allegedly draining several
bottles of alcohol on the vessels Forbes is said to have unlawfully boarded in
Sausalito Yacht Harbor.

Forbes’ family has stated that Forbes is experiencing a mental health crisis,
a claim that seems credible in light of the details, and for an official whose
long public record seems otherwise unblemished. Many Sausalito residents spoke
in support of Forbes at the last City Council meeting, with one longtime
resident asking why law enforcement had chosen to arrest Forbes instead of
bringing her to the appropriate medical facility for an evaluation.

Many more expressed exasperation with the media’s predatory coverage of
Forbes’ arrest.

It was a reasonable question. Why  _was_ the media, even the London-based
_Daily Mail_ , so focused on the Forbes arrest?

In a week when four U.S. military personnel were flown home in caskets, and
the controversial Section 219 of the National Defense Authorization Act was
passed by Congress, Bay Area media largely ignored the issue of the war and
its impacts at home and abroad. Instead, they breathlessly reported that, in
the hours prior to her arrest, Elaine Christina Forbes was alleged to have
emptied a jar of maraschino cherries into a shoebox on someone else’s
expensive yacht.

In other words, media seized on Forbes’ mishap to distract from the actual
news.

Forbes’ unremarkable misdemeanor counts were: prowling (on boats, one count);
unauthorized lodging (on boats, two counts); and petty theft (of clothing, one
count). The “thefted” clothing appears to have been a t-shirt and shorts she
changed into while on one of the boats. (Forbes might not have purloined the
meager outfit had she not been arrested while wearing them.)

Despite the scant damage, no fewer than ten local and national news reporters
and photographers showed up to watch the arraignment on Wednesday afternoon in
Marin County Superior Court. For its part, ABC-7 could find so little else to
report in the Bay Area that they camped outside the courthouse the prior
Tuesday. At one point during a shift change on Tuesday morning, ABC-7 had at
least three very large media trucks stationed outside the courthouse.

**The Men’s Club**

Nearly every reporter and photographer stationed outside the courthouse, eager
to capture a glimpse of Forbes, was male. This was the scene as they began to
trickle in:

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-27-at-2.46.05-PM-680x909.png)

“It’s money,” the Murdoch-controlled  _California Post_ ’s boyishly handsome
photographer smiled sheepishly in explanation for his presence, while the more
aloof _San Francisco Chronicle_ photographer offered no such excuses.

On a bench across from them, excluded from the men’s club, sat Gina Castro,
KQED’s young photographer. “It’s always like this,” she whispered with quiet
resignation, of the men’s club on the other bench that offered her no seat.

One of the local news cameramen had dragged in a comically large video camera
and a tripod. The tripod, which was taller than himself, looked more like
weaponry than video equipment. “Is that a tripod or a rocket launcher?” I’d
softly teased him, as he heaved the massive mount to the security check-in. In
no mood for joking, the cameraman glared at me.

**Why Is KRON4 Dan Kerman Defending Sam Singer?**

On Tuesday (the original day of the arraignment, which had to be moved to
Wednesday), KRON4’s Dan Kerman had paced the hallway outside Courtroom M,
dismissing my gentle suggestion that the media presence might be excessive.

“She’s a public figure,” he asserted testily.

“Okay, but for misdemeanors?” I asked.

Kerman ignored the question.

I then asked Kerman if the hiring of the infamous corporate and police public
relations guru Sam Singer, supposedly a decision by Forbes’ family, might be
counterproductive. Forbes, I pointed out, was already a somewhat sympathetic
figure, and had done no real damage, as opposed to other Singer clients like
Chevron or the Oakland Police Department.

“Singer doesn’t represent the Oakland Police Department,” Kerman huffed,
dodging the question I had posed, “he represents the Oakland Police  _union_.”
And then he sulked off.

But to most victims of the OPD, that was a distinction without much
difference.

And why should Kerman have to be defensive about Singer in the first place?
Weren’t reporters like Kerman supposed to ask tougher questions about PR
masters like Singer? For that matter, shouldn’t they be asking tougher
questions about their own media outlets?

**Why TV News Is Easier Than Actual News**

For all the media coverage of Forbes over the past seven days, you would
hardly know a detail ignored by everyone from the centi-million-dollar
“liberal” KQED to the News Corp-owned  _California Post_. All have “declined”
to report basic points that were published last week in the humble  _Military
Times,_ a publication that is mostly read by U.S. military personnel:

“The war has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $37.5 billion, has led to the deaths
of 18 U.S. service members and injured more than 450 troops. It has killed
thousands of Iranians.”

That’s all: In two sentences that provide four simple truths, the  _Military
Times_ once again demonstrated it is more responsible than The  _San Francisco
Chronicle_ , KQED, or Dan Kerman, all of whom appear to have dodged reporting
on the actual financial cost of the U.S.-Iran War, or summarize U.S.
casualties, or even to consider Iranian casualties.

**A Question of Status And Color**

Almost none of the arraignments I regularly observe in various Bay Area
courthouses elicit any interest from the media, where the majority of the
defendants are, like most who appeared in person before Judge Mayfield later
that day, Black or Latino.

U.S. media accepts, largely without question, that daily arrests and
prosecutions fall primarily on the poor and working-class. The fact that
Forbes, who is white and whose sub-$300K salary is middle-class by Bay Area
standards, was actually arrested for her transgression made her the unlucky
exception to the rule. Yet none of the media coverage could be bothered to
point that out.

A public records request I ran in 2020 retrieved information from the Marin
County District Attorney showing that over a 32-year period (1989 through
2020) the Marin County sheriff and local police departments arrested — and
referred to prosecution — Black and Latino people at a rate far above their
demographic presence in the County.

The law enforcement agencies surrounding Marin City (Marin County Sheriff
Office, Sausalito Police Department, and Mill Valley Police Department)
arrested and referred to prosecution Black people at a rate over  _eight_
times the Black demographic presence in the County from 1989 through 2020.

This reality has been consistently denied by local TV news stations. The
_Marin Independent-Journal_ , which has an official partnership with the
County of Marin, had never bothered to investigate the matter themselves. Nor
has the  _San Francisco Chronicle_ ever reported the disparity.

**Why It’s Important To Report The Media’s Selective and Sensationalistic
Coverage**

When the Forbes story became sensationalized – not only locally but in the
pages of the  _Daily Mail_ and the Murdoch-owned  _California Post_ – I knew
it would be important to watch not only how the case was handled by the media,
but by the special appointment judge in misdemeanor court, Cindee Mayfield.

I was particularly interested in capturing how the media conducted itself in
the courtroom and how it impacted the defendant. When Tuesday’s arraignment
was continued to Wednesday, I immediately went upstairs to submit a media
request in person in room 113. (Several larger outlets only submitted their
media requests the following day.) I returned early to court the following day
to check in with the clerk in Room 113 about the status of my request and was
told there was no answer yet.

**Judge Mayfield Does Not Owe You An Explanation**

The judge in Forbes misdemeanor case is Cindee Mayfield, first appointed to
the Mendocino County Municipal Court in by Republican Governor Pete Wilson in
1997. Mayfield was elevated to Mendocino County Superior Court the following
year due to court consolidation, and retired from Mendocino County Superior
Court in 2025. She is temporarily assigned to Marin County Superior Court.

Beyond that simple outline, very little biographical information is available
on Mayfield online, and  _zero_ biographical information on Mayfield is
available on the Marin County Superior Court website. The message from the
courts is: we don’t expect you to need any background information on judges,
who have absolute immunity, and near-absolute power.

But it was Judge Mayfield who approved so many media requests to record the
Forbes arraignment: from centi-millionaire outlets like KQED, to the
billionaire-owned  _California Post_ , to the Hearst-controlled  _San
Francisco Chronicle_.

Thus, it was Judge Mayfield’s decision to grant media access to News Corp’s
_California Post_ that resulted in the following exploitative headline:
“California city manager’s (sic) Elaine Forbes’ unhinged expression in court
after boozy boat burglary shocked elite locals.”

_That is a striking headline, particularly since the California Post’s
reporter, Annie Gaus, missed the entire arraignment, and had to rely on me to
tell her to go ask the Post’s photographer for his recording. And at no point,
unless you selectively located the most out-of-context split second of video,
did Forbes appear “unhinged”. Forbes looked very nervous, which is fairly
normal for any defendant in court, and tried to ignore the excessive media
presence._

_The headline is not only the fault of the Murdoch-controlled California Post,
a publication that would not be able to exploit the Forbes story as
effectively as it did without media access. The privilege it gained (and
predictably abused) through Judge Mayfield 's permission to record during the
arraignment should raise questions about Mayfield's own lack of judgment:
During the Forbes arraignment, there was more media than audience. And while
media was restricted to the far left side of the courtroom, the sheer number
of them, and their predatory focus on the defendant, constituted a not-
insignificant distraction._

The arraignment was, however, mercifully short. Forbes’ attorney, Randall
Knox, argued that Forbes posed no threat, and Mayfield ordered her released
from jail on the condition that she submitted to evaluation at Marin General.
Why any of that justified so much media coverage remains unexplained.

**Judge Mayfield’s Prejudice**

Most of the reporters granted media access by Judge Mayfield on Wednesday had
never reported from Marin County Superior Court. And only one reporter in
Wednesday’s hearing had reported  _in depth_ on any case in Marin County
Superior Court. That reporter is myself, and yet I was the only reporter whose
media request to record was denied by Judge Mayfield.

The issue is not any absence of prior bylines; I have previously been
published in  _The New Yorker Magazine, The New York Observer,_ and _The New
York Times Magazine._ These are credentials that most reporters at even KQED
do not have.

Nor is the issue one of reach; the Marin County Confidential substack has a
healthy subscription base of attorneys, educators, other journalists, and
elected officials, as well as labor organizers, physicians, nurses, and tech
industry workers.

The principal distinction between myself and the media outlets granted access
by Mayfield appears to be financial: on a near-zero budget and working through
an ongoing physical disability, I have provided more  _detailed_ reporting on
the courts than KRON or the  _California Post_ — or even the  _Marin
Independent-Journal_ , which favors very thin reporting on cases out of Marin
County Superior Court.

Judge Mayfield provided no explanation for why my request was rejected. Nor
did she provide any time for me to appeal the decision. I was only handed the
official paperwork moments before the arraignment started, paperwork that
looked nearly identical to the approved requests.

And neither I nor any of the deputies present had any idea I was not allowed
to record at the time of the arraignment.

By denying my media request to record/publish still photos and video, Judge
Mayfield is restricting the public from seeing the conduct of the moneyed
media outlets in the courtroom.

But  _if_ the public could see what the million-dollar news outlets get away
with, might they start asking for more transparency on their own cases?

And is that why Mayfield denied my request?

The beauty of a temporary judge is that they are even less accountable to the
public than the regular judges. No one in the Clerk’s office nor the Court’s
administrative office had any idea how to appeal such a decision. Email
queries sent on Wednesday to the clerk for Judge Mayfield and to the Court’s
Executive Officer, James Kim, remain unanswered.

The question here is not, “Do cameras belong in court?” since Judge Mayfield
already determined that cameras were warranted. The question is, since cameras
were “warranted”, why was the only camera that would have included the media’s
conduct – and its impact on the defendant – excluded?

_This piece first appeared on[Marin County
Confidential](https://marincountyconfidential.substack.com/p/prowling-media-
goons-what-judge-mayfield)._
